newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen unlikely to cut interest rates in H1.
newsitem.headline: China seen unlikely to cut interest rates in H1.

text.p: China is unlikely to cut interest rates in the first half of 1997, the China Securities newspaper said on Friday.

"From a prudent point of view, the possibility for the central bank to cut interest rates in the first half is very small," it quoted Liu Zhen of brokerage house Shenyin & Wanguo Securities Co as saying.

China cut interest rates last May and again in August to ease credit as inflation fell. The August cut trimmed bank deposit rates by an average of 1.5 percentage points and lending rates by 1.2 percentage points.
Inflation would resurge if the central bank cut rates, he said. "The central bank will be caught in a dilemma if retail price inflation rebounds and exceeds interest rates," Liu said.
China's consumer price inflation was expected to reach about 8.3 percent in 1997, higher than the annual interest rate on one-year bank deposits of 7.47 percent, he said.
An interest rate cut in the first half would also cause sharp fluctuations in financial and stock markets, he said.
China's benchmark retail price inflation rose a year-on-year 2.9 percent in February, down from 3.3 percent in January. China has set an inflation target of 6.0 percent this year.
Inflation was 6.1 percent in 1996, down from 14.8 percent in 1995 and a communist-era high of 21.7 percent in 1994.
